doc.title: David Spinozza interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, NY, September 27, 2025

title: Joey Levine and the jingle business
summary: He became arranger for Joey Levine's jingles for fifteen years, dealt with ad 'suits' and later ran his own jingle company.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: And then you got into the jingle business.

Yeah I got into the jingle business. And that was an interesting thing because a lot of guys wanted to do jingles because jingles the pay scale was really good, you were there for an hour and if the TV spot went national you make residuals, every 13 weeks you get a residual check, you know fifty bucks or something but it added up if you did a lot of them. So whatever, there was this guy named Joey Levine who basically was the Godfather of bubble gum music. He was the one that had that record “Yummy Yummy Yummy I Got Love in My Tummy.” So I met him one day and I said to him, I said, “If I ever met the guy that sang that song I want to kill him, that’s such a ridiculous song.” And I told Joey. And he said, “You know that’s really funny,” he said, “you know I have a jingle business. Do you know how to put music on it, because I don’t know how to write music, I don’t know how to write it down. Do you know how to write it down?” I said yeah. He said, “Cause when I go to the sessions I have to sing parts.” I go, “That’s crazy, Joe.” And I became his arranger. And he wrote all these great spots. I mean he wrote, “I Love My Mounds” you know, and Mounds, and Time Magazine, and all these things and I was the arranger on a lot of those spots because Joey needed somebody to conduct the band and write the stuff out. So for a while – fifteen years – I was in the jingle business just writing out Joey melodies.
I find it fascinating that some of the most memorable hooky things come from as you say, people who can’t write it down.
Yeah. Well we call them hummers.

Hummers. But they come up with – like Joey could come up with a hook in, like a two bar hook that you just say, “How the hell did you come up with that?” You or I could write for a 40-piece orchestra but I couldn’t come up with a hook like that. So there’s different talents within the whole musical world.
Did you have to deal with the ad people who would come in and say things like, “Make it sound yellow.”

Yes. Oh yes, yes, yes. That was one of my least favorite things was dealing with the ad people but you know we called them “the suits.” When the suits get here they’re going to ask for this and they’re going to ask for that, and you have to try to placate the situation and you do the best you can. Yeah. But I didn’t have to go to a lot of those meetings ‘cause it was Joey’s company. Later on when I left Joey I had my own jingle business for

a few years at the tail end of the jingle business. And then I had to go to the meetings and do all that stuff. I didn’t really care for it so I didn’t last very long after that in that business. I didn’t really care for it.
